title: Grumpy cop
subtitle: Norman Reid was 43 years old when police were called to a disturbance in the town of Little Catalina on Aug. 26, 2000.
article: Reid had had a rough life, exacerbated by struggles with schizophrenia. He had been in trouble with the law, and had been in and out of jail.

In fact, Reid had only just been released the month before, and soon started behaving erratically. He was not taking his medication. People witnessed him shouting and flailing his arms. He threatened to kill one young man, and to go after his kids. The man called the RCMP.

When police arrived at his residence, Reid went back inside and came out with a hatchet. The officers tried to calm him down, but Reid snapped and rushed towards one of them. The officer shouted for him to stop. He didn't. Within seconds, Reid was dead on the ground with five bullets in him.
A judicial inquiry into the Reid shooting - and the police shooting of Corner Brook's Darryl Power that same year - found poor mental health services were a key factor in both deaths.

"Those who remembered Norman as a boy appeared to have a sense of him as an individual; they tended to be more compassionate and less likely to regard him with fear. Those who knew him only from his external appearance and the stories they heard often saw him as strange and frightening. There were suggestions that among some youth in the community he was seen as a kind of 'boogie-man' whom it was a challenge to taunt or tease."

Luther's report was a watershed in mental health services in this province. And while the shootings may have been unavoidable, the events also spurred police agencies to take a closer look at how their officers are trained to handle people with mental illness.
Given that fact, it's alarming that a current Royal Newfoundland Constabulary officer could end up chastised for two poorly handled mental health incidents in the span of a few years.

Const. Lisa Harris's behaviour during a May 2013 incident in Torbay was criticized in provincial court this week. Harris yelled and cursed at a man who was clearly suffering a mental crisis. According to CBC, the judge said Harris and her fellow officer had "tunnel vision" about what was happening.

Harris had already been reprimanded for her behaviour in 2009 when she and a fellow officer approached autistic teenager Dane Spurrell in Mount Pearl. Thinking he was drunk, Harris shouted and cursed at Spurrell as he walked aimlessly down a local street.
Policing is demanding work. It requires personal stress management and discipline.
It also requires learning from the price of past missteps while dealing with those suffering from mental health issues.
That hard toll shouldn't have to be paid again because any officer didn't get the message, loud and clear, on behaviour.
